title: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the basic mechanisms of human thinking will in the end turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Validity of the Principle” (from p. 726), p. 733. Scope: human brains and thinking

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.36

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing neuroscience data can evaluate specific simple mechanistic accounts. They cannot identify all mechanisms of thought or establish the broad computational ceiling as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define a target set of cognitive mechanisms and a quantitative simplicity measure, then fit mechanistic computational models to open neural and behavioral datasets and compare them with more complex rivals on held-out interventions and predictions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Current neural datasets have limited resolution and intervention coverage.

Observational equivalence permits many computational models of the same behavior.

'Basic mechanisms' and 'rather simple' lack fixed criteria.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public maps of anatomy and connectivity constrain the hardware of human brains and can test coarse proxies such as locality and cell-type repetition. They do not contain the basic mechanisms of thinking as an identified program, which is what the prediction requires. Several incompatible grains of simplicity fit the same data, so a present analysis would leave the claim itself open.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify the basic operations of a stated cognitive competence and ask whether a simple, fully specified program reproduces them and stays inside Turing computation. Confirmation requires that reduction for the competences counted as basic; a competence that needs a non-recursive step, or that has no simple program at the agreed grain, would refute the corresponding reading.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Rather simple and basic mechanisms can be pitched at the level of a neuron, a cell type, or a cognitive module, with opposite verdicts.

Connectomes and recordings do not identify the program that constitutes thinking.
